Is Your Tucson Property Tax Bill Too High? Here’s What You Can Do

Opening your property valuation notice and seeing a number you do not recognize can be frustrating.

By Reddy Appraisal LLCOctober 22, 20262 min read

IN THIS ARTICLE

Understand the number on your noticeCheck property details and market evidenceReview the deadline before taking actionMore in Property Taxes ↗← All 24 articles

THE SHORT ANSWER

If something looks wrong, act promptly. Pima County generally requires a petition challenging a Notice of Value within 60 days of its mail date, and other notice types may follow different rules.

Understand the number on your notice

Opening your property valuation notice and seeing a number you do not recognize can be frustrating. But in Arizona, a higher tax bill does not necessarily mean the county has overvalued your home. Your bill reflects several factors, including property classification, limited property value, applicable exemptions, and tax rates set by local jurisdictions. The best first step is to review your Pima County Notice of Value and understand exactly which number you are questioning.

Check property details and market evidence

Look closely at the property details the assessor has on file. Is the living area accurate? Are the age, construction features, garage, and other improvements described correctly? Compare the full cash value with recent sales of genuinely similar homes, while accounting for condition, location, and other differences. An incorrect property characteristic or an unsupported full cash value may provide a stronger basis for review than the tax amount alone.

Review the deadline before taking action

If something looks wrong, act promptly. Pima County generally requires a petition challenging a Notice of Value within 60 days of its mail date, and other notice types may follow different rules. Reddy Appraisal LLC can provide independent residential market-value analysis that may help you evaluate the assessor’s estimate and assemble supporting evidence. An appraisal does not guarantee a tax reduction, but informed decisions start with credible information.
